```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
# Same seed as Correlation_Loess.R, so the handout and the lab script print the same resampling results
set.seed(1)
# Print a permutation p-value, writing p < 1/B when no permutation reached the observed value
p_text <- function(p, B) {
    if (p == 0) paste0('p < ', round(1 / B, 3)) else paste0('p = ', round(p, 3))
}
```

# Overview

This lab takes about an hour after a short lecture.
The first three parts use RStudio and the fourth uses Claude.
Each part introduces the idea, its teaching uses, and the R code.

| Minutes | What | Where | Why | How |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0--10 | Lecture | Slides | | |
| 10--25 | Lab Part 1: correlation and simple linear regression, with a bootstrap CI and a permutation p-value | RStudio | Measure linear association and its uncertainty | `cor()` and `lm()`, then two loops around `cor()` |
| 25--40 | Lab Part 2: make a regressogram | RStudio | Let the mean wage change freely across bins | `cut()` and `tapply()` inside the same two loops |
| 40--50 | Lab Part 3: fit a loess curve | RStudio | Draw a smooth curve with a confidence band | `loess()` inside the same two loops |
| 50--65 | Lab Part 4: have Claude review the script | claude.ai | Use AI for checks and extensions | Upload the script and give prompts |

Every part uses the same two loops.
The bootstrap resamples workers to give confidence intervals.
The permutation shuffles one variable to give p-values.
Only the statistic inside the loops changes.

# Correlation and simple linear regression

### What {-}

The covariance is the average product of paired deviations from each variable's mean.
$$\hat{c}_{XY} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} [\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X}] [\hat{y}_{i} - \hat{m}_{Y}] / n.$$
The Pearson correlation rescales the covariance by the two standard deviations.
$$\hat{r}_{XY} = \frac{\hat{c}_{XY}}{\hat{s}_{X} \hat{s}_{Y}}.$$
It has no units and always lies between $-1$ and $1$.
It equals $1$ for a perfect rising line, $-1$ for a perfect falling line, and $0$ when there is no linear association.

Consider the three pairs $(\hat{x}_{i}, \hat{y}_{i})$ in $\{(0, 0.1), (1, 0.3), (2, 0.2)\}$.
The means are $\hat{m}_{X}=1$ and $\hat{m}_{Y}=0.2$.
The correlation is then
$$\begin{aligned}
\hat{c}_{XY} &= \left[(-1)(-0.1) + (0)(0.1) + (1)(0)\right] / 3 = 1/30 \\
\hat{s}_{X} \hat{s}_{Y} &= \sqrt{2/3} \sqrt{2/300} = 2/30 \\
\hat{r}_{XY} &= (1/30) / (2/30) = 1/2.
\end{aligned}$$

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Tiny sample to check by hand
x0_hat <- c(0, 1, 2)
y0_hat <- c(0.1, 0.3, 0.2)
cor(x0_hat, y0_hat)
```

Simple linear regression fits the least squares line
$$\hat{y}_{i} = b_{0} + b_{1} \hat{x}_{i} + \hat{e}_{i}.$$
Its coefficients come from the correlation, the means, and the standard deviations:
$$\hat{b}_{1} = \hat{r}_{XY} \frac{\hat{s}_{Y}}{\hat{s}_{X}}, \qquad \hat{b}_{0} = \hat{m}_{Y} - \hat{b}_{1} \hat{m}_{X}.$$
Its $\hat{R}^{2}$ is the squared correlation between $\hat{y}_{i}$ and the fitted values $\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}} = \hat{b}_{0} + \hat{b}_{1} \hat{x}_{i}$, written $\hat{R}^{2} = \hat{r}_{Y Y^{\mathrm{fit}}}^{2}$.
For a line, this equals $\hat{r}_{XY}^{2}$.
For the three pairs above, $\hat{b}_{1} = (1/2) \sqrt{2/300} / \sqrt{2/3} = 0.05$ and $\hat{b}_{0} = 0.2 - 0.05 = 0.15$.

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Least squares line for the tiny sample
coef(lm(y0_hat ~ x0_hat))
```

### Why {-}

Correlation is the most familiar summary of how two variables move together.
Students meet it early, and it appears in almost every field.
It is also a good first statistic for resampling with two variables.
A textbook interval for a correlation uses the Fisher transformation and normal tables.
The bootstrap loop needs neither.
Simple linear regression turns the correlation into a slope with units, here dollars per hour for each year of experience.

Correlation only measures *linear* association.
The wage data below show why this matters.

### How {-}

The data are 526 US workers from the 1976 Current Population Survey.
For each worker, `exper` is years of potential experience and `wage` is average hourly earnings in 1976 dollars.
They come from the `wooldridge` package, which you install once with `install.packages('wooldridge')`.

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Data: 526 US workers from the 1976 Current Population Survey
xy_hat <- wooldridge::wage1[, c('exper', 'wage')]
colnames(xy_hat) <- c('x_hat', 'y_hat') # x_hat=years of potential experience, y_hat=hourly wage (1976 dollars)
n <- nrow(xy_hat)

# Number of resamples, used in every loop below
B <- 999

# R-squared: the squared correlation between wages and fitted wages
r_squared <- function(y, y_fit) {
    cor(y, y_fit)^2
}

# One color per model in every figure: correlation and linear regression (red), regressogram (green), loess (blue)
# Fitted values use the full color, and confidence intervals use a lighter shade of it
fit_cols <- c(linear=rgb(.8, 0, 0, .8), rgram=rgb(0, .6, 0, .8), loess=rgb(0, 0, .8, .8))
ci_cols <- c(linear=rgb(.8, 0, 0, .3), rgram=rgb(0, .6, 0, .3), loess=rgb(0, 0, .8, .3))
```

The data frame `xy_hat` keeps each worker's experience and wage on the same row.
The number `B` sets how many resamples every loop draws.
The function `r_squared()` computes
$$\hat{R}^{2} = \hat{r}_{Y Y^{\mathrm{fit}}}^{2},$$
the squared correlation between wages and the fitted values from any curve.
For a least squares fit, it is also the share of the variation in wages that the fit explains.
All three parts of the lab use it.

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Scatterplot, with the least squares line in red
plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .25), main=NA,
    xlab='Years of potential experience', ylab='Hourly wage (1976 dollars)')
# Simple linear regression: the least squares line
reg <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat)
abline(reg, col=fit_cols['linear'], lwd=2)
coef(reg)
```

The line rises slowly.
Many workers with little experience earn low wages, and the spread of wages is wide at every level of experience.

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Pearson correlation
xy_cor <- cor(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'], xy_hat[, 'y_hat'])
xy_cor
# The slope is the correlation times the ratio of standard deviations
xy_cor * sd(xy_hat[, 'y_hat']) / sd(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'])
# The squared correlation is the R-squared of the line
xy_cor^2
r_squared(xy_hat[, 'y_hat'], predict(reg))
```

The correlation is $`r round(xy_cor, 3)`$, a weak positive association.
The slope is $`r round(coef(reg)[2], 3)`$, so hourly wages are about $`r round(100 * coef(reg)[2], 1)`$ cents higher for each extra year of experience.
The squared correlation, $`r round(xy_cor^2, 3)`$, is the $\hat{R}^{2}$ of the line.
The line explains about $`r round(100 * xy_cor^2, 1)`\%$ of the variation in wages.

A bootstrap sample for two variables resamples workers, which are the rows of `xy_hat`, with replacement.
Each worker keeps their own experience and wage.
Some workers appear more than once and others do not appear.

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Bootstrap distribution of the correlation and the slope
boot_cor <- rep(NA, B)
boot_slope <- rep(NA, B)
for (b in 1:B) {
    # Resample workers with replacement, keeping each worker's experience and wage together
    xy_b <- xy_hat[sample(n, replace=TRUE), ]
    boot_cor[b] <- cor(xy_b[, 'x_hat'], xy_b[, 'y_hat'])
    boot_slope[b] <- coef(lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_b))[2]
}
```

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Percentile confidence interval: the middle 95% of bootstrap correlations
boot_ci <- quantile(boot_cor, probs=c(.025, .975))
boot_ci
# The same for the slope, in dollars per hour for each year of experience
slope_ci <- quantile(boot_slope, probs=c(.025, .975))
slope_ci

# Histogram of bootstrap correlations, with the observed value in red and the interval in light red
hist(boot_cor, breaks=50, border=NA, freq=FALSE, main=NA,
    xlab='Bootstrap correlation')
abline(v=boot_ci, col=ci_cols['linear'], lwd=2)
abline(v=xy_cor, col=fit_cols['linear'], lwd=2)
```

The $95\%$ interval runs from $`r round(boot_ci[1], 3)`$ to $`r round(boot_ci[2], 3)`$.
It excludes $0$, but the whole interval is small.
The interval for the slope runs from $`r round(100 * slope_ci[1], 1)`$ to $`r round(100 * slope_ci[2], 1)`$ cents per year of experience.

A permutation test imposes the null hypothesis of no association.
It shuffles experience across workers without replacement.
Each wage is then paired with another worker's experience, so any association left is due to chance.

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Permutation distribution of the correlation, imposing no association
perm_cor <- rep(NA, B)
for (b in 1:B) {
    # Shuffle experience without replacement, which breaks the pairing with wages
    xy_p <- xy_hat
    xy_p[, 'x_hat'] <- sample(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'], replace=FALSE)
    perm_cor[b] <- cor(xy_p[, 'x_hat'], xy_p[, 'y_hat'])
}
```

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Two-sided p-value: share of permutations at least as extreme as observed
p_cor <- mean(abs(perm_cor) >= abs(xy_cor))
p_cor

# Histogram of permuted correlations, with the observed value in red
hist(perm_cor, breaks=50, border=NA, freq=FALSE, main=NA,
    xlab='Permuted correlation')
abline(v=xy_cor, col=fit_cols['linear'], lwd=2)
```

The permuted correlations center on zero.
The p-value is the share of them at least as far from zero as the observed correlation, $`r p_text(p_cor, B)`$.
So the correlation is statistically different from zero, even though it is small.

The two loops differ in one line.

| Loop | What `sample()` draws | What it keeps | What it gives |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bootstrap | Rows, with replacement | Each worker's pair | A confidence interval |
| Permutation | Experience only, without replacement | Each variable's values, but not the pairs | A p-value under no association |

The bootstrap asks how much the correlation varies across samples.
The permutation asks how large a correlation chance alone produces.

**Things to try.**

* Change `probs=c(.025, .975)` to `probs=c(.05, .95)` and confirm that the interval narrows.
* Change `replace=FALSE` to `replace=TRUE` in the permutation loop.
  This gives the null bootstrap from the table of resampling types in the book.
  Compare the two p-values.
* Compare the permutation p-value with `cor.test(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'], xy_hat[, 'y_hat'])`.
* Add `method='spearman'` to each `cor()` call to use the rank correlation, and check whether the conclusion changes.

# Regressogram

### What {-}

A regressogram splits $\hat{x}$ into bins and reports the mean of $\hat{y}_{i}$ within each bin.
A bin with midpoint $x$ and half-width $h$ holds the observations with $\hat{x}_{i}$ in $(x-h, x+h]$.
With the dummy variable $\hat{d}_{i}(x,h) = \mathbf{1}(\hat{x}_{i}~\text{in}~(x-h, x+h])$ and the bin count $n(x,h) = \sum_{i} \hat{d}_{i}(x,h)$, the bin mean is
$$\hat{m}_{Y}(x,h) = \frac{\sum_{i} \hat{y}_{i} \hat{d}_{i}(x,h)}{n(x,h)}.$$
Each worker's fitted value $\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}}$ is the mean of their bin.

The same bin means come from OLS.
Regress $\hat{y}_{i}$ on one dummy per bin, with no intercept:
$$\hat{y}_{i} = \sum_{x} b_{0}(x,h) \hat{d}_{i}(x,h) + \hat{e}_{i}.$$
Each worker is in exactly one bin, so the sum of squared errors splits into one sum per bin.
Within a bin, the least squares constant is the mean, so $\hat{b}_{0}(x,h) = \hat{m}_{Y}(x,h)$.

A regressogram is the conditional-mean analog of a histogram.
A histogram counts the observations in each bin of $\hat{x}$.
A regressogram averages $\hat{y}_{i}$ in each bin of $\hat{x}$.

### Why {-}

The regressogram assumes no shape for the relationship.
The bin means can rise, fall, or stay flat from one bin to the next.
Each bin is a group, so it extends the group means that students already compare with two-sample tests and ANOVA.
The bins also make the bandwidth $h$ concrete, which prepares students for loess.

Here, the regressogram finds a hump that the correlation misses.

### How {-}

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Ten-year experience bins, so the half-width is h=5
# The last bin is one year wider, so it also holds the one worker with 51 years
bin_breaks <- c(0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 51)
xy_hat[, 'bin'] <- cut(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'], breaks=bin_breaks)
table(xy_hat[, 'bin'])
```

The bins are ten years wide, so $h=5$.
The first bin holds $`r sum(xy_hat[, 'bin'] == levels(xy_hat[, 'bin'])[1])`$ workers and the last holds $`r sum(xy_hat[, 'bin'] == levels(xy_hat[, 'bin'])[5])`$.

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Regressogram: the mean wage in each bin
bin_means <- tapply(xy_hat[, 'y_hat'], xy_hat[, 'bin'], mean)
bin_means
# The same means are the coefficients from OLS on one dummy per bin, with no intercept
rgram <- lm(y_hat ~ 0 + bin, data=xy_hat)
coef(rgram)
rgram_r2 <- r_squared(xy_hat[, 'y_hat'], predict(rgram))
rgram_r2
```

The coefficients of `rgram` match `bin_means`.
The correlation in `r_squared()` measures variation around the mean wage, so it gives the usual $\hat{R}^{2}$ for the regressogram.
Avoid `summary(rgram)$r.squared` here.
Without an intercept, it measures variation around zero instead, which inflates $\hat{R}^{2}$ to $`r round(summary(rgram)$r.squared, 3)`$.

The mean wage rises from $`r round(bin_means[1], 2)`$ dollars in the first bin to $`r round(bin_means[3], 2)`$ in the middle bin.
It then falls to $`r round(bin_means[5], 2)`$ in the last bin.
The regressogram explains $`r round(100 * rgram_r2, 1)`\%$ of the variation in wages, about $`r round(rgram_r2 / xy_cor^2)`$ times as much as the linear regression.

The bootstrap loop is the same as in Part 1.
It now stores the five bin means from each resample instead of one correlation.

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Bootstrap distribution of each bin mean, one row per resample
boot_bins <- matrix(NA, nrow=B, ncol=length(bin_means))
colnames(boot_bins) <- names(bin_means)
for (b in 1:B) {
    # Resample workers with replacement, then recompute the mean in each bin
    xy_b <- xy_hat[sample(n, replace=TRUE), ]
    boot_bins[b, ] <- tapply(xy_b[, 'y_hat'], xy_b[, 'bin'], mean)
}
```

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Percentile confidence interval for each bin mean, one column per bin
bin_ci <- apply(boot_bins, 2, quantile, probs=c(.025, .975))
round(bin_ci, 2)
```

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Scatterplot with the bin means in green and their intervals in light green
plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .25), main=NA,
    xlab='Years of potential experience', ylab='Hourly wage (1976 dollars)')
bin_lower <- bin_breaks[-length(bin_breaks)]
bin_upper <- bin_breaks[-1]
rect(bin_lower, bin_ci[1, ], bin_upper, bin_ci[2, ], col=ci_cols['rgram'], border=NA)
segments(bin_lower, bin_means, bin_upper, bin_means, col=fit_cols['rgram'], lwd=2)
```

The light green boxes are the $95\%$ intervals for each bin mean.
The interval for the middle bin does not overlap the intervals for the first and last bins.

The permutation loop shuffles experience as in Part 1.
Each worker's bin then has to be recomputed from the shuffled experience.
The statistic is the regressogram $\hat{R}^{2}$.

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Permutation distribution of the regressogram R-squared, imposing no association
perm_rgram_r2 <- rep(NA, B)
for (b in 1:B) {
    # Shuffle experience, then recompute each worker's bin from the shuffled value
    xy_p <- xy_hat
    xy_p[, 'x_hat'] <- sample(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'], replace=FALSE)
    xy_p[, 'bin'] <- cut(xy_p[, 'x_hat'], breaks=bin_breaks)
    rgram_p <- lm(y_hat ~ 0 + bin, data=xy_p)
    perm_rgram_r2[b] <- r_squared(xy_p[, 'y_hat'], predict(rgram_p))
}
```

```{r}
#| eval: true
# One-sided p-value, since R-squared is never negative
# A value of 0 means no permutation reached the observed value, so p < 1/B
p_rgram <- mean(perm_rgram_r2 >= rgram_r2)
p_rgram

# Histogram of permuted R-squared values, with the observed value in green
hist(perm_rgram_r2, breaks=50, border=NA, freq=FALSE, main=NA,
    xlim=range(c(perm_rgram_r2, rgram_r2)),
    xlab='Permuted regressogram R-squared')
abline(v=rgram_r2, col=fit_cols['rgram'], lwd=2)
```

$\hat{R}^{2}$ is never negative, and only large values are evidence against no association.
So the p-value counts the permutations at or above the observed value, and is one-sided.

Even with no association, the bin means differ a little by chance.
So the permuted $\hat{R}^{2}$ values sit above zero, with an average of $`r round(mean(perm_rgram_r2), 3)`$.
The permutation distribution shows how much pattern the bins find in pure noise.
Here $`r sum(perm_rgram_r2 >= rgram_r2)`$ of the $`r B`$ permuted values reach the observed $`r round(rgram_r2, 3)`$, so $`r p_text(p_rgram, B)`$.

**Things to try.**

* Use five-year bins, so $h=2.5$, with `bin_breaks <- c(seq(0, 45, by=5), 51)`.
  Check `table()` for small bins and rerun the bootstrap.
  Bins with few workers tend to get wider intervals.
* With the five-year bins, rerun the permutation loop.
  Compare the average permuted $\hat{R}^{2}$ with the one for ten-year bins.
  More bins find more pattern in pure noise.
* Shuffle wages instead of experience with `xy_p[, 'y_hat'] <- sample(xy_hat[, 'y_hat'], replace=FALSE)`.
  Then the bins need no recomputing.
  Confirm the p-value is similar.
* Replace `mean` with `median` in both `tapply()` calls to get binned medians.

# Loess

### What {-}

Loess (locally estimated scatterplot smoothing) fits a weighted regression at each design point $x$.
Nearby workers get more weight and distant workers get less or none.
The lab sets `degree=1`, so `loess()` fits a local line within each window, by weighted least squares:
$$\min_{b_{0}(x,h), b_{1}(x,h)}~ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\hat{y}_{i} - b_{0}(x,h) - b_{1}(x,h) \hat{x}_{i} \right]^{2} k_{T}\left(\hat{x}_{i}, x, h\right).$$
The fitted value at $x$ is the local mean
$$\hat{m}_{Y}(x,h) = \hat{b}_{0}(x,h) + \hat{b}_{1}(x,h) x.$$
As with the regressogram, $\hat{m}_{Y}(x,h)$ estimates the mean wage near experience $x$.
This is the local linear regression from the book, with tricube weights and an adaptive bandwidth.
R's default, `degree=2`, adds a quadratic term $b_{2}(x,h) \hat{x}_{i}^{2}$.

The weights come from the tricube kernel,
$$k_{T}\left(\hat{x}_{i}, x, h\right) = \left(1 - \left|\frac{\hat{x}_{i} - x}{h}\right|^{3}\right)^{3} \mathbf{1}\left(|\hat{x}_{i} - x| \leq h\right).$$
A worker at $x$ gets weight $1$.
The weight falls smoothly to $0$ at distance $h$, and workers farther away get none.

A regressogram uses fixed bins with the same half-width $h$ everywhere.
Loess slides the window along $x$ and sets its width so that it always holds the same share of the data.
This share is the `span`.
Formally, $h$ is the distance from $x$ to its $q$-th nearest $\hat{x}_{i}$, where $q = \lfloor \text{span} \times n \rfloor$.
With the default `span=0.75`, each local fit uses the nearest $q = `r floor(.75 * n)`$ of the $`r n`$ workers.
Where data are sparse, the window widens.

The code below computes the loess fit by hand at $x = 21$, which Part 3 finds is the peak of the curve.

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Loess by hand at one design point
x0 <- 21
d <- abs(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'] - x0)
# Bandwidth: the distance to the q-th nearest worker, with q = floor(span * n)
h <- sort(d)[floor(.75 * n)]
h
# Tricube weights
k_t <- ifelse(d <= h, (1 - (d / h)^3)^3, 0)
# Weighted least squares with a line in experience
reg_x0 <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat, weights=k_t)
predict(reg_x0, newdata=data.frame(x_hat=x0))
```

The window around $x = `r x0`$ reaches $h = `r h`$ years.
The window around $x = 45$, where workers are scarcer, reaches $h = `r sort(abs(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'] - 45))[floor(.75 * n)]`$ years.

### Why {-}

Loess draws a smooth curve without choosing a functional form in advance.
Students can build the band around the curve with the same bootstrap loop, so they can also explain it.
The span plays the role of $h$, so loess also shows the bias-variance tradeoff (see Extensions).
The permutation test with $\hat{R}^{2}$ works unchanged.

### How {-}

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Local linear loess with the default span, which uses the nearest 75% of workers at each x
reg_lo <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat, degree=1)
lo_r2 <- r_squared(xy_hat[, 'y_hat'], predict(reg_lo))
lo_r2
```

The squared correlation between wages and the loess fit is $`r round(lo_r2, 3)`$.

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Predict at every year of experience in the data
pred_design <- data.frame(x_hat=seq(min(xy_hat[, 'x_hat']), max(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'])))
y_fit_lo <- predict(reg_lo, newdata=pred_design)
# Experience at the peak of the fitted curve
pred_design[which.max(y_fit_lo), 'x_hat']
```

The fitted curve peaks at $`r pred_design[which.max(y_fit_lo), 'x_hat']`$ years of experience.
There, `loess()` gives $`r round(max(y_fit_lo), 3)`$ dollars, close to the hand computation above.
By default, `loess()` computes the fit exactly at a few design points and interpolates between them, so the two differ slightly.

The bootstrap loop refits loess on each resample.
It stores the predictions at every design point, so each column of `boot_lo` is one bootstrap curve.

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Bootstrap distribution of the loess curve, one column per resample
boot_lo <- matrix(NA, nrow=nrow(pred_design), ncol=B)
for (b in 1:B) {
    # Resample workers with replacement, refit loess, and predict at every design point
    xy_b <- xy_hat[sample(n, replace=TRUE), ]
    reg_lo_b <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_b, degree=1)
    boot_lo[, b] <- predict(reg_lo_b, newdata=pred_design)
}
```

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Pointwise 95% confidence band
# Loess does not extrapolate, so a resample that misses the most experienced workers gives NA there
lo_cb <- apply(boot_lo, 1, quantile, probs=c(.025, .975), na.rm=TRUE)

# Scatterplot with the loess curve in blue and its band in light blue
plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .25), main=NA,
    xlab='Years of potential experience', ylab='Hourly wage (1976 dollars)')
polygon(c(pred_design[, 'x_hat'], rev(pred_design[, 'x_hat'])),
    c(lo_cb[1, ], rev(lo_cb[2, ])), col=ci_cols['loess'], border=NA)
lines(pred_design[, 'x_hat'], y_fit_lo, col=fit_cols['loess'], lwd=2)
```

The band is the middle $95\%$ of the bootstrap curves at each design point.
It is narrow where there are many workers and wider at the edges.

Loess does not extrapolate beyond the data it was fit on.
A resample that misses the one worker with the most experience cannot predict there, so `predict()` returns `NA`.
This happens in $`r round(100 * mean(is.na(boot_lo[nrow(boot_lo), ])))`\%$ of resamples at $`r max(pred_design[, 'x_hat'])`$ years.
The option `na.rm=TRUE` drops those resamples, so the band at the edge uses fewer curves.

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Permutation distribution of the loess R-squared, imposing no association
perm_lo_r2 <- rep(NA, B)
for (b in 1:B) {
    # Shuffle experience without replacement, then refit loess
    xy_p <- xy_hat
    xy_p[, 'x_hat'] <- sample(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'], replace=FALSE)
    reg_lo_p <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_p, degree=1)
    perm_lo_r2[b] <- r_squared(xy_p[, 'y_hat'], predict(reg_lo_p))
}
```

```{r}
#| eval: true
# One-sided p-value, as for the regressogram
p_lo <- mean(perm_lo_r2 >= lo_r2)
p_lo

# Histogram of permuted R-squared values, with the observed value in blue
hist(perm_lo_r2, breaks=50, border=NA, freq=FALSE, main=NA,
    xlim=range(c(perm_lo_r2, lo_r2)),
    xlab='Permuted loess R-squared')
abline(v=lo_r2, col=fit_cols['loess'], lwd=2)
```

A flexible curve also finds some pattern in pure noise, so the permuted values average $`r round(mean(perm_lo_r2), 3)`$.
Here $`r sum(perm_lo_r2 >= lo_r2)`$ of the $`r B`$ permuted values reach the observed $`r round(lo_r2, 3)`$, so $`r p_text(p_lo, B)`$.

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Summary: the same two loops for three descriptions of the data
round(cbind(
    R_squared=c(Linear=xy_cor^2, Regressogram=rgram_r2, Loess=lo_r2),
    p_value=c(p_cor, p_rgram, p_lo)), 3)
```

All three p-values are small.
But the linear regression explains far less of the variation than the regressogram or loess.
The correlation is weak because the relationship is a hump, not a line.
A weak correlation does not mean a weak relationship.

**Things to try.**

* Refit loess with `span=0.3` and with `span=2`, in both `loess()` calls of the fit and the bootstrap.
  A smaller span gives a wigglier curve and a wider band.
* Change `degree=1` to `degree=2` in each `loess()` call to fit local quadratics instead of local lines.
* Add `control=loess.control(surface='direct')` to the first `loess()` call, so it computes the fit exactly at every design point.
  The value at the peak then matches the hand computation in What.
* Rerun the permutation loop with `span=0.3` and compare the average permuted $\hat{R}^{2}$ with the default span.
* Add the regressogram to the loess figure with `segments(bin_lower, bin_means, bin_upper, bin_means, col=fit_cols['rgram'], lwd=2)`.

# Extensions

## Marginal effects

### What {-}

Write the loess curve from Part 3 as $\hat{m}_{Y}(x)$, dropping $h$ for short.
The marginal effect of experience at $x$ is the slope of this curve, $d \hat{m}_{Y}(x) / dx$.
The mean marginal effect averages this slope over workers, $\sum_{i} [d \hat{m}_{Y}(\hat{x}_{i}) / dx] / n$.
The marginal effect at the mean is the slope at the mean experience, $d \hat{m}_{Y}(\hat{m}_{X}) / dx$.
When the curve is not a line, the linear regression coefficient $\hat{b}_{1}$ is generally neither one.

### Why {-}

Economic theory stresses marginal effects, such as diminishing returns.
Loess is consistent: with more data and a smaller span, its slope approaches the true marginal effect.
Simple linear regression is not, unless the true curve is a line.
The bootstrap gives an interval for each marginal effect with the same loop as before.

### How {-}

The code below finds the slope with a small step of $0.01$ years on each side of $x$.

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Slope of a loess curve at x, from a small step on each side of x
# At the edges of the data the curve was fit to, the step uses only the side inside the data
lo_slope <- function(lo_fit, x, eps=.01) {
    x_range <- range(lo_fit[['x']])
    x_lo <- pmax(x - eps, x_range[1])
    x_hi <- pmin(x + eps, x_range[2])
    y_lo <- predict(lo_fit, newdata=data.frame(x_hat=x_lo))
    y_hi <- predict(lo_fit, newdata=data.frame(x_hat=x_hi))
    (y_hi - y_lo) / (x_hi - x_lo)
}

# Mean marginal effect: the slope at each worker's experience, averaged over workers
me_mean <- mean(lo_slope(reg_lo, xy_hat[, 'x_hat']))
me_mean
# Marginal effect at the mean: the slope at the mean experience
me_at_mean <- lo_slope(reg_lo, mean(xy_hat[, 'x_hat']))
me_at_mean
# Compare with the linear regression coefficient from Part 1
coef(reg)[2]
```

The linear regression coefficient is $`r round(coef(reg)[2], 3)`$ dollars per hour for each year of experience.
The mean marginal effect is $`r round(me_mean, 3)`$, and the marginal effect at the mean is $`r round(me_at_mean, 3)`$.

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Bootstrap both marginal effects: resample workers, refit loess, and recompute each one
boot_me <- matrix(NA, nrow=B, ncol=2)
for (b in 1:B) {
    xy_b <- xy_hat[sample(n, replace=TRUE), ]
    reg_lo_b <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_b, degree=1)
    boot_me[b, 1] <- mean(lo_slope(reg_lo_b, xy_b[, 'x_hat']))
    boot_me[b, 2] <- lo_slope(reg_lo_b, mean(xy_b[, 'x_hat']))
}

# Percentile confidence interval for each, one column per marginal effect
me_ci <- apply(boot_me, 2, quantile, probs=c(.025, .975))
colnames(me_ci) <- c('Mean marginal effect', 'Marginal effect at the mean')
round(me_ci, 3)
# The same interval for the linear regression coefficient, from Part 1
round(slope_ci, 3)
```

The $95\%$ interval for the mean marginal effect runs from $`r round(me_ci[1, 1], 3)`$ to $`r round(me_ci[2, 1], 3)`$.
It excludes the linear regression coefficient.
The interval for the marginal effect at the mean is much wider, from $`r round(me_ci[1, 2], 3)`$ to $`r round(me_ci[2, 2], 3)`$, and it includes the linear regression coefficient.
A slope at one point varies more from sample to sample than an average of slopes over all workers.

## Bandwidth and the bias-variance tradeoff

### What {-}

The span decides how many workers each local fit uses.
A wide span uses many workers, so the curve changes little from sample to sample (low variance).
But a wide span can smooth over real bends (high bias).
A narrow span follows bends closely (low bias), but it also chases noise (high variance).

### Why {-}

Students can see both sides of the tradeoff in one figure.
The bootstrap band shows the variance directly.

### How {-}

The code below fits a wide span and a narrow span, each with its own bootstrap band.

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
# A wide and a narrow span, each its own model with a color not used above
spans <- c(2, 0.3)
span_cols <- c(rgb(.6, 0, .6, .8), rgb(.9, .5, 0, .8))
band_cols <- c(rgb(.6, 0, .6, .3), rgb(.9, .5, 0, .3))

plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .25), main=NA,
    xlab='Years of potential experience', ylab='Hourly wage (1976 dollars)')
for (s in seq_along(spans)) {
    # Loess fit with this span
    reg_s <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat, span=spans[s], degree=1)
    # Bootstrap curves with the same span, one column per resample
    boot_s <- matrix(NA, nrow=nrow(pred_design), ncol=B)
    for (b in 1:B) {
        xy_b <- xy_hat[sample(n, replace=TRUE), ]
        reg_s_b <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_b, span=spans[s], degree=1)
        boot_s[, b] <- predict(reg_s_b, newdata=pred_design)
    }
    # Pointwise 95% band, then the fitted curve on top
    cb_s <- apply(boot_s, 1, quantile, probs=c(.025, .975), na.rm=TRUE)
    polygon(c(pred_design[, 'x_hat'], rev(pred_design[, 'x_hat'])),
        c(cb_s[1, ], rev(cb_s[2, ])), col=band_cols[s], border=NA)
    lines(pred_design[, 'x_hat'], predict(reg_s, newdata=pred_design),
        col=span_cols[s], lwd=2)
}
legend('topright', title='Span', legend=spans,
    col=span_cols, lwd=2, bty='n')
```

With span $2$, every local fit uses all the workers.
The curve smooths over the hump, and its band is narrow.
As the span grows further, the curve approaches the least squares line from Part 1.
With span $0.3$, the curve picks up more local wiggles and its band is much wider.

The bands show variance, but not bias, because the true curve is unknown.
The book separates the two by treating a large dataset as a known population.

## A confidence interval for the peak

### What {-}

The peak is the years of experience at which the loess curve is highest.
It depends on the whole curve, and no simple formula gives its standard error.

### Why {-}

The bootstrap needs no formula, only a new statistic.
The curves in `boot_lo` from Part 3 already contain everything needed.

### How {-}

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Experience at the peak of each bootstrap curve
boot_peak <- apply(boot_lo, 2, function(y_fit) pred_design[which.max(y_fit), 'x_hat'])
peak_hat <- pred_design[which.max(y_fit_lo), 'x_hat']

# Percentile confidence interval for the peak
peak_ci <- quantile(boot_peak, probs=c(.025, .975))
peak_ci

# Histogram of bootstrap peaks, one bar per year of experience
hist(boot_peak, breaks=seq(min(boot_peak) - .5, max(boot_peak) + .5, by=1),
    border=NA, freq=FALSE, main=NA, xlab='Bootstrap peak (years of experience)')
abline(v=peak_ci, col=ci_cols['loess'], lwd=2)
abline(v=peak_hat, col=fit_cols['loess'], lwd=2)
```

The $95\%$ interval for the peak runs from $`r peak_ci[1]`$ to $`r peak_ci[2]`$ years.
That is wide, because the curve is nearly flat over much of the middle of the experience range.
Small changes in the sample can then move the peak a long way.
Most bootstrap peaks fall between $19$ and $23$ years, with a smaller group between $25$ and $28$ years.
A formula-based interval would hide this shape.

## Association is not causation

The hump describes different workers at one point in time.
It does not show that a given worker's wage first rises and then falls with experience.
In a single cross-section, workers with more experience also belong to earlier cohorts.
In 1976, workers with $40$ years of potential experience started their careers around the 1930s.
They differ from younger workers in schooling and in other ways that also affect wages.
Potential experience is also not the same as years actually worked.
Following the same workers over time would help separate these explanations.

## More extensions

You can adapt this document for your courses.
Additional material is openly available online.

* [Statistics of Association (Ch. 14)](https://jadamso.github.io/Rbooks/02_14_Associations.html#hypothesis-testing): bootstrap and permutation distributions of the correlation, and Falk's median correlation for data with outliers.
* [Simple Regression (Ch. 15)](https://jadamso.github.io/Rbooks/02_15_SimpleRegression.html): the least squares line, $\hat{R}^{2}$, and bootstrap and permutation tests for the slope.
* [Association is not Causation (Ch. 16)](https://jadamso.github.io/Rbooks/02_16_NotCausation.html): correlation without causation, and causation without correlation.
* [Local Regression (Ch. 17)](https://jadamso.github.io/Rbooks/02_17_LocalRegression.html#regressograms): regressograms, piecewise regression, and sliding windows.
* [Gradients (Ch. 18)](https://jadamso.github.io/Rbooks/02_18_Gradients.html#confidence-bands): loess confidence bands, gradients, and tests that the gradients are zero.
* [Working with AI (Appendix A)](https://jadamso.github.io/Rbooks/04_A_WorkingWithAI.html): the full eight-step review.
  This lab uses four of those steps.
